title-group.article-title: Pluviatolide Attenuates Type I Hypersensitivity through Regulation of Mast Cell Activation

abstract.p: This study examined the inhibitory effects of pluviatolide, a lignan derived from Podophyllum hexandrum, on mast cell activation and IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity, focusing on FcεRI-dependent and calcium-mediated pathways. Using bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) and rat basophilic leukemia (RBL)-2H3 cells, we found that pluviatolide significantly decreased β-hexosaminidase release and suppressed the expression and secretion of TNF-α and IL-6 in a concentration-dependent manner, without causing cytotoxicity. While we initially hypothesized that it would selectively modulate antigen-specific FcεRI signaling, pluviatolide also inhibited degranulation induced by calcium ionophore and thapsigargin, indicating its effects extend to receptor-independent, Ca2+-dependent activation mechanisms. Immunoblot analyses revealed decreased phosphorylation of proximal kinases (Lyn, Syk), adaptor proteins (LAT, PLCγ1), MAPKs (ERK1/2, JNK, p38), and NF-κB p65. In a passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model, oral administration of pluviatolide significantly reduced Evans blue extravasation and mast cell degranulation in ear tissues. These findings demonstrate that pluviatolide suppresses both early and late-phase mast cell responses through multi-nodal inhibition of activation pathways, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic candidate for both IgE-mediated and non-IgE-mediated allergic disorders.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Immediate-type hypersensitivity, also known as type I hypersensitivity, refers to a rapid immune response triggered by exposure to specific allergens (Abbas et al., 2025; Galli et al., 2008; Hamilton, 2010). Mast cells play a central role in this process by becoming activated when allergens cross-link immunoglobulin E (IgE) that is bound to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on their surface (Galli and Tsai, 2012; Gurish and Austen, 2012; Kinet, 1999). This activation triggers the rapid release of preformed mediators, including histamine, proteases, and pro-inflammatory cytokines. These substances contribute to hallmark allergic manifestations such as increased vascular permeability, smooth muscle constriction, and localized inflammation (Mukai et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023). These physiological outcomes are closely linked to allergic diseases, including asthma, anaphylaxis, and atopic dermatitis (Theoharides and Kalogeromitros, 2006). The prevalence of allergic disorders is rising worldwide, and many current treatment options are limited by suboptimal efficacy or adverse effects. This situation has prompted the search for novel agents with improved safety profiles. (Dierick et al., 2020; Ogulur et al., 2021). Naturally derived compounds, especially lignans, have garnered attention for their anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties (Jang et al., 2022). Lignans are plant-derived polyphenolic compounds that modulate immune responses and alleviate allergic symptoms by inhibiting mast cell activation and the release of mediators. (Farhan et al., 2024).

Pluviatolide is a lignan compound originally isolated from the roots of Podophyllum hexandrum. It has been reported to exhibit anti-inflammatory, antitumor, cytotoxic, and antispasmodic activities (Decembrino et al., 2020; Grigore, 2017; Hazra and Chattopadhyay, 2016). However, its effects on mast cell–mediated allergic responses have not been explored. Mast cells, located at mucosal and dermal surfaces, act as immune sentinels and play a crucial role in initiating and amplifying type I hypersensitivity reactions (Zhang and Kurashima, 2021). Modulating mast cell activation is a logical strategy for controlling both the immediate and late phases of allergic inflammation (Katsoulis-Dimitriou et al., 2020).

This study aimed to evaluate the anti-allergic potential of pluviatolide by examining its effects on mast cell degranulation, cytokine secretion, and intracellular signaling pathways. We utilized both in vitro and in vivo models to assess the compound’s ability to suppress FcεRI-mediated responses and to investigate the underlying mechanisms. Specifically, we explored whether the inhibitory effects of pluviatolide were limited to antigen-specific, receptor-dependent pathways or if they also extended to calcium-dependent, receptor-independent activation. The findings offer new insights into the pharmacological potential of pluviatolide as a promising therapeutic agent for allergic diseases linked to mast cell hyperactivation.

sec.title: Reagents
sec.p: Pluviatolide (Cat. No. HY-N9926) was purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Dallas, TX, USA). Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) 1640 medium, Minimum Essential Medium (MEM), fetal bovine serum (FBS), and other standard reagents for cell culture were obtained from Gibco/Life Technologies (Rockville, MD, USA). Dinitrophenyl (DNP)-specific IgE and DNP-human serum albumin (HSA) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Additional reagents, including ionomycin, thapsigargin, and p-nitrophenyl-N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminide (p-NAG), were also obtained from Sigma-Aldrich.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: Male BALB/c mice (5–6-weeks-old) were purchased from Orient Bio (Gyeonggi-do, Korea). The mice were housed in a specific pathogen-free environment at 22 ± 1°C with 55 ± 10% humidity, with ad libitum access to food and water. All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Dong-A University (Approval No. DIACUC-21-11) and conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines.

sec.title: Mast cell culture
sec.p: Bone marrow cells were harvested from the femurs and tibiae of BALB/c mice and cultured in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 µg/mL penicillin-streptomycin, 4 mM L-glutamine, 25 mM HEPES, 0.05 mM β-mercaptoethanol, and 10 ng/mL interleukin-3 (PeproTech, Cranbury, NJ, USA) for 4 weeks. Mature bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) were identified by flow cytometric analysis using anti-c-Kit and anti-FcεRI antibodies (eBioscience, San Diego, CA, USA) and showed >95% purity. Rat basophilic leukemia (RBL)-2H3 cells (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) were cultured in MEM supplemented with 15% FBS, 100 U/mL penicillin-streptomycin, and 4 mM L-glutamine in a 5% CO2 humidified incubator at 37°C.

sec.title: Cell viability assay
sec.p: BMMCs (5×104 cells/well) were seeded in 96-well plates and treated with various concentrations of pluviatolide for 4 h. Cell viability was measured using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (Dojindo Laboratories, Kumamoto, Japan) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: β-Hexosaminidase release assay
sec.p: BMMCs (2.5×105 cells/well) were sensitized with 100 ng/mL DNP-IgE for 4 h, washed, and resuspended in Tyrode’s buffer. Cells were pretreated with pluviatolide for 30 min, then stimulated with 50 ng/mL DNP-HSA for 15 min. Supernatants and cell lysates (0.1% Triton X-100) were incubated with p-NAG for 1 h at 37°C, and the reaction was stopped with carbonate buffer. Absorbance was measured at 405 nm, and degranulation was calculated as the percentage of β-hexosaminidase released into the supernatant relative to the total. For calcium-dependent degranulation, BMMCs were pretreated with pluviatolide and stimulated with 1 μM ionomycin or 300 nM thapsigargin; degranulation was evaluated as above. For RBL-2H3 cells, 2.5×105 cells/well were sensitized with 20 ng/mL DNP-IgE for 12 h, pretreated with pluviatolide in Siraganian buffer, and stimulated with 25 ng/mL DNP-HSA for 15 min.

sec.title: Quantitative real-time PCR
sec.p: BMMCs (1×106 cells/well) were sensitized with 50 ng/mL DNP-IgE for 4 h, pretreated with pluviatolide for 30 min, and stimulated with 50 ng/mL DNP-HSA for 3 h. Total RNA was extracted using the AccuPrep Universal RNA Extraction Kit (Bioneer, Daejeon, Korea) and reverse-transcribed with CycleScript RT PreMix (Bioneer). qPCR was performed with SYBR Green Master Mix (KAPA Biosystems) on a Thermal Cycler Dice Real Time System III (Takara, Japan). Primer sequences for Tnfa, Il6, and Gapdh are listed in Table 1. Real-time polymerase chain reaction was performed in the following order 40 cycles, 15 s at 95°C, 1 min at 60°C. The comparative CT method was used for relative quantification.

sec.title: Measurement of release of TNF-α and IL-6
sec.p: BMMCs (1×106 cells/well) were sensitized and pretreated as described above, then stimulated with 50 ng/mL DNP-HSA for 3 h. Culture supernatants were collected, and TNF-α and IL-6 levels were determined using ELISA kits (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: Western blot analysis
sec.p: IgE-sensitized BMMCs (2×106 cells/well) were pretreated with pluviatolide and stimulated with DNP-HSA (50 ng/mL) for 15 min. The reaction was stopped on ice for 5 min, cells were lysed in NP-40 lysis buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitor buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Nonidet P-40, 10% glycerol, 60 mM octyl β-glucoside, 10 mM NaF, 1 mM Na3VO4, 1 mM phenylmethyl sulfonyl fluoride, 2.5 mM nitrophenyl phosphate, 0.7 µg/mL pepstatin, and a protease-inhibitor cocktail tablet). Protein concentrations were determined using the Bradford assay (BioRad, Hercules, CA, USA). Equal amounts of protein were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE), transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes, and blocked with 5% BSA in TBS-T. Membranes were incubated with primary antibodies against phospho-LYN (Tyr507), phospho-SYK (Tyr319), phospho-LAT (Tyr191), phospho-PLCγ1 (Tyr783), phospho-Akt (Thr308), phospho-ERK1/2 (Thr202/Tyr204), phospho-JNK (Thr183/Tyr185), phospho-p38 (Thr180/Tyr182), phospho-NF-κB p65 (Ser536), total Syk, LAT, AKT, ERK1/2, JNK, p38, NF-κB p65 purchased from Cell Signaling Technology, Inc. (Danvers, MA, USA) and LYN, LAT, PLCγ1 purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Dallas, Texas, USA). The secondary antibodies used were rabbit polyclonal antibody and mouse monoclonal antibody purchased from Cell Signaling Technology, Inc. (Danvers, MA, USA). The reacted membrane was identified using Chemi-doc (Azure C300, Azure Biosystems, Dublin, CA, USA).

sec.title: Passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) model
sec.p: BALB/c mice were sensitized by intradermal injection of 20 ng DNP-IgE into both ears. After 24 h, pluviatolide (20 mg/kg) or cetirizine (50 mg/kg) was orally administered. PCA was induced via intravenous injection of 100 μg DNP-HSA mixed with 5 mg/kg Evans blue. After 1 h, mice were euthanized, and ears were collected. Evans blue was extracted with formamide at 63°C for 24 h, and absorbance was measured at 620 nm.

sec.title: Histological analysis
sec.p: Excised ear tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde. The fixed ear tissue was dehydrated with ethanol and paraffinized. The paraffin tissue was cut into 5 μm-thick sections and stained with 1% toluidine blue. To determine the percentage of degranulated mast cells in ear tissues, the data were expressed as the ratio of the number of degranulated mast cells to the total number of mast cells present in the tissue. For histological quantification, ear tissue was collected from the same anatomical region on one side of each mouse. Two paraffin-embedded sections were prepared from each sample, yielding a total of 12 sections (6 mice×2 sections). These sections were used for mast cell counting and degranulation analysis.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data are presented as mean ± SEM from at least three independent experiments. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 7 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test was applied for multiple group comparisons, statistical significance was defined as *p<0.05, **p<0.01, and ***p<0.001.

sec.title: Inhibitory effect of pluviatolide on β-hexosaminidase release in mast cells
sec.p: Upon activation, mast cells release a wide array of preformed mediators, including histamine, proteases, and cytokines, which drive the acute phase of allergic responses (Blank et al., 2014; Gilfillan and Beaven, 2011; Krystel-Whittemore et al., 2015; Mukai et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023). To assess the anti-allergic potential of pluviatolide, we first examined its effect on IgE-antigen-induced degranulation in BMMCs. The chemical structure of pluviatolide (C20H20O6) is depicted in Fig. 1A. Cell viability was evaluated using a CCK-8 assay, which revealed no cytotoxicity at concentrations ranging from 25 to 100 µM (Fig. 1B). Mast cell degranulation was quantified by measuring the release of β-hexosaminidase, a well-established marker of granule exocytosis. (Fukuishi et al., 2014). Pluviatolide inhibited β-hexosaminidase release in a concentration-dependent manner, with an IC50 of approximately 35.06 µM (Fig. 1C). Similar inhibitory effects were noted in both BMMCs (Fig. 1D) and RBL-2H3 cells (Fig. 1E). Following preincubation with pluviatolide, BMMCs were stimulated with antigen and subjected to several washing steps. The inhibition of β-hexosaminidase release was completely reversed after washing, with degranulation levels returning to those of the antigen-stimulated controls (Fig. 1F). This indicates that the effect of pluviatolide is reversible and reliant on its presence during stimulation.

sec.title: Suppression of calcium-dependent degranulation by pluviatolide
sec.p: Calcium signaling plays a pivotal role in mast cell activation and subsequent (Cohen et al., 2015; Holowka et al., 2016). To determine whether pluviatolide influences calcium-driven activation, we stimulated BMMCs with ionomycin, a calcium ionophore, or thapsigargin, an inhibitor of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+-ATPase (Huber et al., 2000; Iskarpatyoti et al., 2022). Pluviatolide treatment significantly reduced β-hexosaminidase release induced by ionomycin (33% reduction) and thapsigargin (41% reduction) at a concentration of 100 µM, compared to the dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) control (Fig. 2). These results indicate that the inhibitory effect of pluviatolide is not limited to antigen-specific FcεRI signaling; rather, it extends to receptor-bypassing, Ca2+-dependent activation mechanisms, suggesting that downstream exocytotic machinery is an additional target.

sec.title: Inhibition of TNF-α and IL-6 production by pluviatolide
sec.p: Given the central role of TNF-α and IL-6 in amplifying and sustaining allergic inflammation, we evaluated the impact of pluviatolide on cytokine expression and secretion. Antigen-stimulated BMMCs pretreated with pluviatolide exhibited a concentration-dependent reduction in Tnfa and Il6 transcript levels, as assessed by qRT-PCR (Fig. 3A, 3B), along with corresponding decreases in TNF-α and IL-6 secretion measured by ELISA (Fig. 3C, 3D). These findings suggest that pluviatolide suppresses not only immediate degranulation but also late-phase production of pro-inflammatory mediators, potentially limiting the progression from acute to chronic allergic inflammation.

sec.title: Inhibitory mechanism of pluviatolide on FcεRI signaling cascade
sec.p: To clarify the intracellular mechanism by which pluviatolide suppresses mast cell activation, we assessed its impact on FcεRI-mediated signal transduction (Gilfillan and Rivera, 2009). Immunoblot analysis revealed a reduction in the phosphorylation of the proximal tyrosine kinases Lyn and Syk, as well as the downstream adaptor proteins LAT and PLCγ1 (Fig. 4A, 4B).

Next, we examined the downstream signaling pathways that influence cytokine production and contribute to cellular responses during allergic inflammation. (Gilfillan and Tkaczyk, 2006). Pluviatolide reduced antigen-induced activation of MAPKs, including ERK1/2, JNK, and p38, while also decreasing the phosphorylation of NF-κB p65, a key regulator of inflammatory cytokine expression (Fig. 4C, 4D). By targeting both upstream effectors (Lyn/Syk) and downstream pathways (MAPKs and NF-κB) in the signaling cascade, pluviatolide functions as a multi-node modulator of mast cell activity. These findings support the hypothesis that pluviatolide interrupts mast cell activation at a signaling level that occurs before calcium influx and the induction of cytokine genes.

sec.title: Pluviatolide attenuates passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in vivo
sec.p: To evaluate whether pluviatolide exerts anti-allergic effects in vivo, we established a PCA model in BALB/c mice. Before determining the final oral dose, we referenced previous in vivo studies of structurally related lignans, which commonly reported efficacy within a range of 10 to 25 mg/kg in mice (Park et al., 2025). Based on this reference range, we conducted a preliminary dose-finding experiment using doses of 1, 5, and 20 mg/kg to identify an effective working concentration. In this pilot test, only the 20 mg/kg dose produced a reproducible reduction in PCA responses (data not shown), and this dose was therefore adopted for subsequent in vivo evaluation. Oral administration of pluviatolide (20 mg/kg, 200 μL per mouse) significantly reduced antigen-induced vascular permeability, as quantified by Evans blue extravasation (Fig. 5A, 5B). Histological analysis of toluidine blue-stained ear tissue sections revealed a marked reduction in mast cell degranulation in pluviatolide-treated mice compared to vehicle controls (Fig. 5C, 5D). These in vivo findings are consistent with our in vitro results, which show that pluviatolide suppresses IgE-mediated vascular permeability and mast cell degranulation in peripheral tissues. Together with the cellular data, these results indicate that pluviatolide exerts anti-allergic effects across multiple experimental levels, supporting further evaluation of its therapeutic potential in models of allergic disease.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Allergic diseases, such as atopic dermatitis, asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergies, affect a significant portion of the global population and are becoming increasingly prevalent (Alska et al., 2025; Dierick et al., 2020; Ogulur et al., 2021; Shin et al., 2023). Despite advances in understanding their immunopathogenesis, treatment strategies primarily focus on symptomatic relief and allergen avoidance. However, complete avoidance is often impractical due to the widespread presence and variability of allergens. Mast cells are key effector cells in IgE-mediated allergic reactions, and their activation triggers the rapid release of inflammatory mediators that contribute to both the acute and chronic phases of allergic inflammation (Abassi et al., 2004).

In this study, we identified pluviatolide as a potential inhibitor of mast cell activation. Pluviatolide significantly reduced antigen-induced degranulation in both murine bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) and RBL-2H3 cells, demonstrating no cytotoxicity at effective concentrations (Fig. 1B, 1D, 1E). The IC50 for β-hexosaminidase inhibition in BMMCs was approximately 35 µM (Fig. 1C), indicating moderate potency with a favorable safety margin. Since β-hexosaminidase release is a well-established marker of mast cell degranulation (Fukuishi et al., 2014; Moon et al., 2014; Staats et al., 2013), these findings suggest that pluviatolide has a direct inhibitory effect on one of the earliest effector events in IgE-mediated hypersensitivity. Furthermore, the inhibitory effect was reversible after repeated washing, indicating that pluviatolide does not persist within cells and that its activity requires continuous presence during stimulation. This characteristic may also suggest a favorable safety profile (Fig. 1F).

We initially hypothesized that pluviatolide would selectively inhibit FcεRI-mediated activation triggered by IgE-antigen engagement. However, we found that the compound also reduced degranulation induced by ionomycin and thapsigargin, which bypass the receptor and directly disrupt intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis (Fig. 2) (Huber et al., 2000; Iskarpatyoti et al., 2022). This finding suggests that the inhibitory mechanism extends beyond receptor-proximal events to include the modulation of downstream calcium-dependent exocytotic machinery. This dual-pathway inhibition implies that pluviatolide may be effective in allergic responses driven by both classical IgE-mediated mechanisms and non-IgE-dependent mast cell activation, which can occur in certain forms of chronic urticaria, drug hypersensitivity, and pseudo-allergic reactions.

We evaluated the impact of pluviatolide on cytokine expression and release, which are indicative of late-phase mast cell responses. When antigen/IgE-stimulated bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) were treated with pluviatolide, we observed a concentration-dependent decrease in the mRNA expression of Tnfa and Il6, as well as a reduction in the secretion of TNF-α and IL-6 (Fig. 3). These cytokines play a crucial role in tissue inflammation and the recruitment of immune cells, contributing to the enhancement and persistence of allergic responses by promoting leukocyte infiltration and sustaining local inflammation (Namakanova et al., 2022; Stenvinkel et al., 2005; Theoharides and Kalogeromitros, 2006).

Their inhibition indicates that pluviatolide has the potential to mitigate both the acute manifestations of type I hypersensitivity and the progression to chronic allergic inflammation. Mechanistically, the inhibitory effects of pluviatolide were linked to decreased phosphorylation of the proximal tyrosine kinases Lyn and Syk, as well as the adaptor proteins LAT and PLCγ1 (Fig. 4A, 4B). Additionally, pluviatolide reduced the activation of both the MAPK pathways (ERK1/2, JNK, and p38) and NF-κB p65 (Fig. 4C, 4D), two key signaling modules that work together to promote inflammatory cytokine expression and enhance mast cell responses. These pathways play a crucial role not only in acute activation events but also in the transcriptional programs associated with the late phase of allergic inflammation (Gilfillan and Rivera, 2009). Together, the coordinated suppression of these signaling cascades provides a mechanistic basis for pluviatolide’s ability to inhibit both early degranulation and cytokine production in mast cells.

The in vivo relevance of our findings was validated using a PCA mouse model, where oral administration of pluviatolide significantly reduced antigen-induced vascular leakage and mast cell degranulation in ear tissues. Given that vascular hyperpermeability and the activation of tissue-resident mast cells are hallmark features of local type I hypersensitivity (AhYoung et al., 2020; Kunder et al., 2011), these results strongly suggest that the inhibitory effects of pluviatolide observed in vitro translate into a physiologically relevant suppression of allergic responses in vivo.

To our knowledge, this is the first report demonstrating that pluviatolide, a naturally derived lignan, suppresses IgE-mediated mast cell activation through both receptor-dependent and calcium-mediated pathways in multiple experimental systems. Although its anti-inflammatory and anti-tumor activities have been previously described (Decembrino et al., 2020; Grigore, 2017; Hazra and Chattopadhyay, 2016), its role in allergic regulation has not been addressed. Our findings support the further development of pluviatolide and its structurally related derivatives as potential treatments for mast cell-driven allergic diseases. Future research should aim to clarify its direct molecular targets, pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic profiles, and its selectivity for mast cells compared to other immune cell types. Additionally, studies should assess its effectiveness in systemic anaphylaxis and chronic allergy models to determine its translational potential. Overall, pluviatolide effectively suppresses mast cell-mediated allergic responses by inhibiting both early-phase degranulation and late-phase cytokine production through the blockade of key FcεRI-associated signaling pathways (Fig. 6). These effects were consistently observed both in vitro and in vivo, indicating its promise as a lead compound for developing novel therapeutics aimed at treating IgE-mediated and non-IgE-mediated allergic disorders.

Proposed mechanism of Pluviatolide-mediated regulation of FcεRI signaling in mast cells. Pluviatolide attenuates Lyn kinase activation, thereby reducing phosphorylation of downstream signaling molecules such as Syk, LAT, MAPKs, and PLCγ1. In addition, pluviatolide suppresses mast cell activation induced by Ca2+-dependent, receptor-independent stimuli, suggesting that its inhibitory action is not restricted to IgE-FcεRI signaling. Collectively, these effects result in reduced degranulation, cytokine production, and release of allergic mediators. Lyn, tyrosine-protein kinase Lyn; Syk, spleen tyrosine kinase; LAT, linker for activation of T cells; PLCγ1, phospholipase C gamma 1; PI3K, phosphoinositide 3-kinase; Akt, protein kinase B; MAPKs, mitogen-activated protein kinases.
